summary: Describes the Expedited Forwarding per-hop behavior in Differentiated Services, a way for routers to treat marked packets as a premium service with low delay and low loss. It was replaced by RFC 3246.

eli5.summary: Think of a fast lane at the airport that lets certain packets skip the queue so they arrive quickly and smoothly.

subtitle: A premium service that prioritizes certain packets to minimize delay and loss.

tldr.problem: Networks carry many types of traffic with different requirements. Some applications like voice calls need very low delay and loss, while others like file transfers can tolerate more delay.
tldr.mechanism: Expedited Forwarding (EF) marks special packets with a codepoint in their IP header, and routers ensure these marked packets leave quickly without queuing, at a guaranteed minimum rate.
tldr.outcome: Applications can build a premium service that behaves like a dedicated point-to-point connection even though it shares the network with other traffic. RFC 3246 provides a more complete specification.

facts.label: Measurement interval
facts.value: At least one maximum-size packet time at configured rate

today: RFC 2598 defines the Expedited Forwarding per-hop behavior as a Proposed Standard. It was replaced by RFC 3246, which provides a more complete specification for EF.

sections.title: The Problem of Network Delays
sections.content:
Network nodes that support Differentiated Services (DiffServ) use a codepoint in the IP header to select a per-hop behavior—the forwarding treatment a packet receives at each router. Expedited Forwarding (EF) is a per-hop behavior that allows routers to treat marked packets as a premium service.

Queues form when traffic arrives faster than a router can forward it. To provide low loss, low latency and low jitter for certain traffic (such as voice calls), a network must ensure that aggregate traffic never queues. This requires two things: configuring routers to forward the aggregate at a guaranteed rate, and conditioning incoming traffic to never exceed that rate.
sections.eli5: When lots of people show up at once, they have to wait in line. But if we promise a group of people a fast lane with a certain speed, they never have to wait if they arrive at that speed or slower.

sections.title: How Expedited Forwarding Works
sections.content:
The EF PHB guarantees that packets marked for it leave a router at or above a configurable minimum rate, independent of how much other traffic is using the router. The router MUST guarantee an average rate at least equal to the configured rate, measured over any interval longer than the time to send one maximum-size packet at that rate.

Routers can implement EF using different mechanisms: a priority queue (if higher-priority queues are also rate-limited), a weighted round-robin scheduler where EF gets a fixed share of bandwidth, or a CBQ scheduler that gives EF priority up to the configured rate. Routers MUST limit the maximum EF rate to prevent EF traffic from starving other traffic.
sections.eli5: The router watches how fast packets arrive and how fast they leave, and makes sure the special packets always get enough bandwidth to stay on schedule.

sections.title: Configuring and Using EF
sections.content:
Routers implementing EF must allow administrators to set a configurable minimum departure rate and a maximum rate (which may be the same). The recommended codepoint for EF is 101110 in the IP Differentiated Services field.

EF packets can be remarked at domain boundaries only to other codepoints that satisfy the EF PHB, and SHOULD NOT be demoted to other per-hop behaviors. When EF packets are tunneled, the outer tunnel packets must also be marked as EF. EF coexists with other per-hop behaviors in the same router or domain as long as the minimum rate guarantee is maintained.
sections.eli5: Each router needs to know the minimum speed it promises, and special packets keep their special marking as they travel through different network regions.

sections.title: Security and Denial of Service
sections.content:
Without protection, an attacker could send large amounts of EF-marked traffic to consume the fast lane. To prevent this, the edge of each Differentiated Services domain MUST strictly police all EF-marked packets to a negotiated rate with the upstream domain. Packets exceeding this rate are dropped.

If two adjacent domains have not negotiated an EF rate, the downstream domain MUST treat all EF packets as unauthorized and drop them. The RFC recommends that unexpected drops (either at the edge or in the EF queue) be logged as possible security violations or configuration errors.
sections.eli5: Just like an airport fast lane needs to check that people have tickets for it, routers check that EF traffic is allowed and drop packets that are trying to cheat the system.

sections.title: Virtual Leased Line Service
sections.content:
Combining the EF PHB with traffic shaping at network boundaries can create a service that appears to the endpoints like a dedicated point-to-point connection, called a Virtual Leased Line. The EF PHB provides the forwarding guarantee, while edge routers shape traffic to ensure it never exceeds the negotiated rate.

This service has been successfully deployed on DOE's ESNet backbone using weighted-round-robin queuing in Cisco routers. Early tests showed that TCP flows over a VLL service achieved throughput very close to the subscribed rate, making the shared network appear like a dedicated connection.
sections.eli5: By combining fast-lane packets with careful traffic control at the edges, you can make part of a shared network feel like you have your own private connection.
